f_kartli_kakheti.name: Kartli-Kakheti (eastern Georgia, incl. Borchali, Kazakh-Shamshadil, Lori)
f_kartli_kakheti.geometry_note: Modern Kakheti, Kvemo Kartli, Tbilisi, Shida Kartli, Mtskheta-Mtianeti, plus the Muslim-ruled marches that were in the Georgian king's orbit in 1800 (Qazakh/Agstafa/Tovuz = Kazakh-Shamshadil sultanates; Armenian Tavush and Lori). Samtskhe-Javakheti (Ottoman Akhaltsikhe pashalik), Imereti, Guria, Samegrelo and Abkhazia are excluded: no Tehran claim found, although Gulistan Art. 3 names them. Frontier zone: borders of the marches are approximate.

f_shuragel_shirak.name: Shuragel (Shirak plain, Gyumri area)
f_shuragel_shirak.geometry_note: Modern Shirak province. Shuragel/Shoragol was a Muslim sultanate on the Georgian-Erivan frontier; its exact extent is uncertain.

f_ganja_khanate.name: Ganja Khanate
f_ganja_khanate.geometry_note: Ganja city and surrounding districts (Goranboy, Goygol, Shamkir, Dashkasan, Gadabay, Samukh, Naftalan). Pre-1880 frontier zone: khanate limits fluid; Qazakh/Shamshadil are in f_kartli_kakheti.

f_karabakh_khanate.name: Karabakh Khanate (excluding Shusha), incl. Zangezur
f_karabakh_khanate.geometry_note: Lowland and highland Karabakh plus Zangezur (Syunik); Shusha is a separate region so that the 1826 hold-out can be shown. Frontier zone; khanate edges (esp. Zangezur/Meghri and the Kura lowlands) are approximate.

f_shusha.name: Shusha (fortress and district)
f_shusha.geometry_note: Shusha city + Shusha district: Karabakh's capital, held by a Russian garrison and Armenian defenders through the 1826 Persian siege.

f_shaki_khanate.name: Shaki Khanate
f_shaki_khanate.geometry_note: Shaki city and district, Qabala and Oghuz. Qakh/Zaqatala/Balakan (Elisu sultanate, Jar-Belokan) are NOT mapped: only nominal Safavid-era overlordship found, no distinct Qajar claim.

f_shirvan_khanate.name: Shirvan Khanate (incl. Salyan lowlands)
f_shirvan_khanate.geometry_note: Shamakhi, Agsu, Ismailli, Gobustan and the Kura-Aras lowlands (Hajigabul to Salyan/Neftchala). Khanate had 17 mahals; boundaries with Quba, Baku and Mughan are approximate.

f_baku_khanate.name: Baku Khanate
f_baku_khanate.geometry_note: Baku city, Absheron peninsula and Sumqayit.

f_quba_khanate.name: Quba Khanate
f_quba_khanate.geometry_note: Quba, Qusar, Khachmaz, Khizi, Shabran, Siazan. Quba and Derbent were united under Shaykh Ali Khan 1802-06.

f_derbent_khanate.name: Derbent Khanate (Derbent coast, southern Dagestan)
f_derbent_khanate.geometry_note: Derbent city and district plus Magaramkent and Suleyman-Stalsky; the khanate was a narrow coastal strip.

f_south_dagestan.name: Southern Dagestan (Tabasaran, Kaytag, Kura, Akhty, Rutul)
f_south_dagestan.geometry_note: Highland districts south of the Shamkhal/Avar lands. Extent of Tehran's nominal claim is poorly defined; Chechnya and northern Dagestan were never claimed.

f_talysh_lankaran.name: Talysh Khanate, northern part ceded at Gulistan (Lankaran, Astara-north, Masally, Mughan lowlands)
f_talysh_lankaran.geometry_note: Split of the Talysh khanate: Gulistan gave Russia 'the greater part of Talysh north of the Astara river' and 'the better part of Moghan'; the remainder (Zuvand highlands) went in 1828. Districts allocated to each cession are approximate; the 1813-18 delimitation commission fixed the real line.

f_talysh_zuvand.name: Talysh Khanate remainder (Zuvand highlands) ceded at Turkmenchay
f_talysh_zuvand.geometry_note: Lerik and Yardymli (Zuvand). Turkmenchay Art. 4 draws the line 'along the mountain chain separating Zuvand and Arsh'. Which districts were Persian between 1813 and 1828 is approximate.

f_erivan_khanate.name: Erivan Khanate (incl. Surmali/Igdir, Sharur-Daralayaz)
f_erivan_khanate.geometry_note: Yerevan, Ararat, Armavir, Kotayk and Aragatsotn plains plus Igdir (Surmali) and the Sharur-Sadarak lowlands. Gokcha/Sevan (Gegharkunik) is a separate region; Vayots Dzor is with Nakhchivan; Lori/Shirak with Georgia. Approximate mahal limits.

f_gokcha_sevan.name: Gokcha / Lake Sevan zone (Gegharkunik)
f_gokcha_sevan.geometry_note: Modern Gegharkunik. The northern shore was seized by Russia in 1825 on the argument that Gulistan's vague frontier gave it the district.

f_nakhchivan_khanate.name: Nakhchivan Khanate (Nakhchivan, Julfa, Vayots Dzor)
f_nakhchivan_khanate.geometry_note: Modern Nakhchivan districts except Ordubad (separate) and Sharur/Sadarak (Erivan), plus Vayots Dzor, which Wikipedia attributes to the khanate.

f_ordubad.name: Ordubad
f_ordubad.geometry_note: Ordubad district, on the Aras; part of the Nakhchivan khanate but occupied separately.

f_abbasabad_bridgehead.name: Abbasabad bridgehead (right bank of the Aras)
f_abbasabad_bridgehead.geometry_note: Tiny parcel inside modern Iran. Centre taken at the Aras border near the Aras dam/reservoir (~39.07N 45.40E); true fortress position uncertain by several km.

f_firuzeh_firyuza.name: Firuzeh (Firyuza oasis and district, Kopet Dag)
f_firuzeh_firyuza.geometry_note: Oasis and adjacent district ceded in 1893. Centre approximate; radius is illustrative (district area not found). NOT the Firuzeh county of Razavi Khorasan.

f_turkmen_akhal_tejen.name: Akhal-Atek oases and Tejen (Turkmen lands under the Kopet Dag)
f_turkmen_akhal_tejen.geometry_note: Gokdepe, Ak Bugday, Baherden, Kaka (Abivard), Babadayhan and Tejen: the Tekke oases whose overlordship Tehran claimed until 1881. The Iranica phrase is 'lands beyond the Tejen... Meyhana, Abivard, Nesa and Marv'.

f_old_sarakhs_north.name: Old Sarakhs (Serakhs, north/east bank)
f_old_sarakhs_north.geometry_note: Serakhs district across the Hari Rud from Iranian Sarakhs.

f_bayezid.name: Bayezid / Toprakkale district (Ottoman, held by Iran 1821-23)
f_bayezid.geometry_note: Dogubayazit (Bayezid), Diyadin, Caldiran, Eleskirt (Toprakkale); the extent of Abbas Mirza's occupation is approximate.

f_baban_sulaymaniyah.name: Baban emirate / Shahrizor (Sulaymaniyah)
f_baban_sulaymaniyah.geometry_note: Modern Sulaymaniyah governorate as proxy for the Baban principality (Sulaymaniyah, Shahrizor, Qara Dagh); real extent shifted.

f_zohab_lowlands.name: Zohab lowlands (west), around Khanaqin
f_zohab_lowlands.geometry_note: Khanaqin district as proxy for the 'lowlands in the western part of the province of Zohab' ceded in 1847. The 1847 text gives no coordinates; the line was fixed by the 1913-14 commission.

f_zohab_transferred.name: Zohab 'Transferred Territory' (1913)
f_zohab_transferred.geometry_note: Location and extent are NOT verified: sources say Persia evacuated a 'Transferred Territory' in the Zohab sector under the 1913 Protocol (Anglo-Persian Oil Co. rights safeguarded), the area around Qasr-e Shirin/Naft Khaneh east of the Sirwan; Qasr-e Shirin town stayed Persian.

f_kotur_zone.name: Kotur-neighbourhood strip ceded to Turkey in 1932
f_kotur_zone.geometry_note: Iranica: the 1932 line left Turkey 'ninety square miles in the neighbourhood of Kotur' (between Guirberan and Kuch Dagh). Exact location not verified.

f_little_ararat_zone.name: Little Ararat zone ceded to Turkey in 1932
f_little_ararat_zone.geometry_note: A British diplomat's cable put the northern zone at about 60 square miles, giving Turkey control of all Lesser Ararat; exact line not verified.

f_muhammarah_khizr.name: Muhammarah (Khorramshahr) and Khizr island (Abadan)
f_muhammarah_khizr.geometry_note: Inside modern Iran. Included only because its sovereignty was disputed with the Ottomans before 1847; the internal agent may overlay the Ka'b/Muhaisin sheikhdom (indirect) for 1812-1925.

f_shatt_east_half.name: Shatt al-Arab (Arvand Rud), eastern half-channel, Khaiin canal to the sea
f_shatt_east_half.geometry_note: The river is an international boundary river; the thalweg (median line of the main navigable channel) was agreed in 1975. Strip is schematic.

f_shatt_muhammara_anchorage.name: Muhammarah anchorage reach (Khaiin canal to the Karun mouth)
f_shatt_muhammara_anchorage.geometry_note: 'The modern port and anchorage of Muhammara, above and below the junction of the river Karun with the Shatt al-Arab' (1913 Protocol); extent of the reach is approximate.

f_shatt_abadan_thalweg.name: Shatt al-Arab opposite Abadan (thalweg segment of 1937)
f_shatt_abadan_thalweg.geometry_note: Segment where the 1937 treaty moved the boundary from the Iranian low-water mark to the thalweg.

f_irq_majnoon.name: Majnoon Islands (Hawizeh marshes)
f_irq_majnoon.geometry_note: Operation Kheibar captured ~160 km2 with ~50 oil wells.

f_irq_halabja.name: Halabja district (Iraqi Kurdistan)
f_irq_halabja.geometry_note: Halabcha district; Operation Dawn 10 also took Dojileh and Khurmal.

f_herat_state.name: Herat and Farah (Herat principality)
f_herat_state.geometry_note: Modern Herat and Farah provinces as the Sadozai principality and its dependencies (Ghurian, Sabzawar/Shindand, Lash-Juwayn). Ghurian was not split out: no reliable separate chronology found.

f_sistan_afghan.name: Afghan Sistan (Nimruz: Chakhansur, Kang, Zaranj)
f_sistan_afghan.geometry_note: Modern Nimruz province (Goldsmid's 'Outer Seistan', the right/east bank of the Helmand and lands beyond).

f_makran_kech_panjgur.name: Kech and Panjgur (Makran)
f_makran_kech_panjgur.geometry_note: Modern Kech and Panjgur districts: the Gichki/Kalat lands assigned to Kalat by the 1871 Goldsmid line (Panjgur, Parum, Buleda, Mand, Tump, Kech, Dasht). Gwadar (Omani) not mapped.

f_kuhak.name: Kuhak district
f_kuhak.geometry_note: Small district awarded to Kalat in 1871, reclaimed by Iran, occupied May 1874, formally Iranian in 1896. Radius illustrative.

f_mirjaveh.name: Mirjaveh frontier parcel
f_mirjaveh.geometry_note: Disputed 1896-1905 between the Holdich line's 'blue' reading and Persian possession; radius illustrative.

f_chabahar.name: Chabahar (Omani appanage)
f_chabahar.geometry_note: Inside modern Iran; included because it was a Muscat/Omani possession.

f_sirri.name: Sirri island
f_sirri.geometry_note: Inside modern Iran; parcel because the Qasimi deputy-governors of Lengeh held it.

i_mashhad_area.name: Mashhad district (Nader Mirza 1796-1803; Salar revolt 1848-50)
i_mashhad_area.geometry_note: Mashhad county plus Binalud. Nader Mirza and Hasan Khan Salar each held the shrine city; neither man's wider reach is mappable to counties (see i_salar_khorasan_wide). Modern Mashhad county is far larger than the 19th-century city+oasis.

i_salar_khorasan_wide.name: Sabzevar-Neyshabur zone held by Hasan Khan Salar (1848-49)
i_salar_khorasan_wide.geometry_note: Sources only name Sabzevar and Neyshabur (Nishapur) as retaken by the government in March 1849; the neighbouring counties are inferred. Wikipedia also lists Bojnurd and Qa'en as dominated by Salar; those belong to separate regions (i_bojnurd_shadlu, i_qaenat_alam) and are omitted to avoid overlap.

i_torbat_qarai.name: Torbat-e Heydarieh (Qara'i principality)
i_torbat_qarai.geometry_note: Iranica: a Qara'i principality "stretching from the gates of Mashhad to Khaf" with Torbat-e Heydarieh as capital. Counties are an approximation of that corridor; the real boundary fluctuated with the chiefs' power.

i_quchan_zafaranlu.name: Quchan (Za'faranlu Kurdish ilkhanate)
i_quchan_zafaranlu.geometry_note: Za'faranlu Kurds held Quchan/Chenaran (Iranica names Chenaran as their seat in the Qajar period). Faruj and Dargaz are approximations of their pastoral range on the Atrek/Kopet-Dag side.

i_bojnurd_shadlu.name: Bojnurd-Esfarayen (Shadlu Kurdish ilkhanate)
i_bojnurd_shadlu.geometry_note: Iranica: Shadlu controlled Esfarayen and Bojnurd; Kurds of other tribes (Keyvanlu, Bicaranlu, Zangalanlu...) held the remainder of northern Khorasan. Counties are the modern North Khorasan block minus Quchan-side units.

i_qaenat_alam.name: Qa'enat (Khozeimeh/'Alam amirate)
i_qaenat_alam.geometry_note: Core Qa'enat districts of modern South Khorasan. Tabas/Ferdows/Boshruyeh were at times attached to the Qa'enat governorship but are left out. Sistan is separate (i_sistan).

i_tabas_khans.name: Tabas (hereditary Zangu'i/Vakil khans)
i_tabas_khans.geometry_note: Tabas county only; the historical Tabas-e Masina/Gilaki governorship may have reached Ferdows/Boshruyeh margins, not mapped.

i_sistan.name: Sistan (Persian Sistan)
i_sistan.geometry_note: Modern Iranian Sistan = the 1872 Goldsmid award line (west of the Helmand). Before 1872 the Sistan lowlands were ruled by local chiefs and disputed with Afghanistan; the Iranian county set is only the part that ended up in Iran.

i_baluch_bampur_saravan.name: Persian Baluchistan: Bampur, Fahraj, Sarbaz, Dizzak, Saravan
i_baluch_bampur_saravan.name_fa: بلوچستان (بمپور، فهرج، سرباز، دیزک و سراوان)
i_baluch_bampur_saravan.geometry_note: Western/central Baluchistan, the domain of the Bampur governorate and the Barakzai (Baranzai) chiefs. Counties approximate old districts Bampur, Dizzak, Sarbaz, Geh and Qasr-e Qand named by Iranica.

i_baluch_sarhad.name: Sarhad (Khash, Mirjaveh, Zahedan/Dozdab)
i_baluch_sarhad.geometry_note: Northern Baluch highland (Sarhad) along the British Baluchistan frontier; the Dozdab (Zahedan) railhead lies in Zahedan county. Boundary with the Bampur block approximate.

i_chabahar_oman.name: Chabahar bay (Omani dependency until 1872)
i_chabahar_oman.geometry_note: Only the Chabahar-Dashtiari coast was concerned. The two modern counties are much larger than the Omani-claimed bay and its Jadgal-controlled hinterland.

i_pesyan_khorasan.name: Khorasan under Col. Pesyan (1921)
i_pesyan_khorasan.geometry_note: Razavi Khorasan minus the Quchan/Dargaz Kurdish zone (which fought Pesyan). Wikipedia calls the entity the Autonomous Government of Khorasan with Mashhad as capital; actual reach beyond Mashhad, Neyshabur and Sabzevar is poorly documented.

i_turkmen_sahra.name: Turkmen Sahra (Yomut and Goklen)
i_turkmen_sahra.geometry_note: Plain between the Atrek, the Caspian shore and the Gorgan river. Yomut lived west/south of Gonbad, Goklen to the east; Galikash/Minudasht/Azadshahr were mixed or Persian-settled and are omitted. Tribal ranges were seasonal and fuzzy.

i_shahsevan.name: Shahsevan country (Ardabil, Moghan, Sabalan)
i_shahsevan.geometry_note: Winter pastures in Moghan (Parsabad, Bilehsavar, Garmi) and summer pastures on the Sabalan slopes (Meshkinshahr, Ardebil, Khalkhal) = modern Ardabil Province. Shahsevan also ranged into Sarab (East Azerbaijan; left out to avoid overlap with Azadistan) and, per Iranica, between Zanjan and Qazvin; only the core block is mapped.

i_gilan.name: Gilan
i_gilan.geometry_note: Whole of modern Gilan province. Jangali control (1915-20) was concentrated in Fuman, Shaft, Siahkal, Rasht hinterland, Lahijan and Rudbar; the coast (Anzali, Rasht) was repeatedly held by Russian/British garrisons or the Soviets, so single-province treatment is a simplification.

i_tabriz_area.name: Tabriz and the Jolfa road
i_tabriz_area.geometry_note: Russian garrisons held Tabriz and the Julfa-Tabriz axis; the 1908-09 siege concerned the Tabriz city and its quarters. Modern Tabriz county is larger than the 1909 city.

i_azadistan_khiabani.name: Azadistan (Khiabani) - East Azerbaijan
i_azadistan_khiabani.geometry_note: Khiabani's movement claimed the whole province of Azerbaijan; Iranica says only a few towns stayed under Tehran or tribal chiefs, but only Tabriz's control is firmly documented. East Azerbaijan is used as the maximum plausible extent.

i_urmia_khoy_salmas.name: Urmia-Khoy-Salmas plain
i_urmia_khoy_salmas.geometry_note: Counties around Lake Urmia's west shore that saw the Russian withdrawal (1918), the Assyrian-Kurdish war and the Ottoman reoccupation (June-July 1918).

i_ottoman_border_strip_1906.name: Ottoman-occupied frontier strip west of Lake Urmia (1906-12)
i_ottoman_border_strip_1906.geometry_note: Schematic strip; see custom.note. A county-union would grossly overstate the occupation.

i_russian_occupation_azerbaijan_1827.name: Azerbaijan occupied by Russia (1827-28) except Khoy
i_russian_occupation_azerbaijan_1827.geometry_note: Tabriz (13 Oct 1827), Urmia (28 Jan 1828), Ardabil (8 Feb 1828) are the documented captures; Marand/Jolfa (the Aras crossing and road), Khoy and Salmas are inferred as lying on the Russian line. The Turkmenchay treaty tied evacuation to indemnity instalments, so the occupied area shrank by stages. Verification: Khoy split off to i_russian_khoy_1828, which Russia kept as security for the indemnity long after the rest of Azerbaijan was evacuated.

i_qazvin_zanjan_norperforce.name: Qazvin-Zanjan sector of Norperforce
i_qazvin_zanjan_norperforce.geometry_note: Norperforce had its HQ at Qazvin, the main body at Manjil (Gilan, inside i_gilan), a battalion at Zanjan and posts along the Manjil-Qazvin road. The occupation was a road-line, not a full area.

i_sanandaj_zone.name: Sanandaj / Ardalan Kurdistan (and southern Kurdistan in 1979-83)
i_sanandaj_zone.geometry_note: Modern Kurdistan Province. The Ardalan vilayet centred on Sanandaj (Senneh) and Bijar, Kamyaran, Marivan, Sarvabad; Saqqez and Baneh were Mukri/Ardalan marchland and are the least certain inclusions for 1800-67.

i_kurdistan_kermanshah_border_1979.name: Paveh-Javanrud-Ravansar (Kermanshah Kurdistan, 1979-83)
i_kurdistan_kermanshah_border_1979.geometry_note: Kurdish-majority counties of Kermanshah province in which Kurdish forces took garrisons in March 1979 and fought in Aug-Sept 1979.

i_mahabad_zone.name: Mahabad zone (Mukriyan; Republic of Mahabad; KDPI core)
i_mahabad_zone.geometry_note: Mukriyan = south of Lake Urmia incl. Mahabad, Bukan, Sardasht, Oshnaviyeh. The 1946 republic is usually described as Mahabad, Bukan, Naghadeh, Piranshahr, Oshnavieh, with Sardasht often added. Miandoab was Azeri-majority and contested; it is left out here and put under ADP.

i_ubeydullah_1880.name: Area overrun by Sheikh Ubeydullah (1880)
i_ubeydullah_1880.name_fa: مناطق تصرف‌شده به دست شیخ عبیدالله (۱۲۵۹)
i_ubeydullah_1880.geometry_note: Sources say Sauj Bulaq (Mahabad) and Maragheh were taken and Urmia held out; Miandoab lies between them. Raiding extended widely west of Lake Urmia, but held ground is not mappable.

i_simko_core.name: Shikak country (Simko), Salmas-Chehriq-Ushnu
i_simko_core.geometry_note: Chehriq fortress (Salmas county) was Simko's base; Qotur/Baradost/Ushnu and the Mamash/Mangur/Piran pastures are covered by the neighbouring counties. Extent varied month to month.

i_simko_extended.name: Mahabad-Miandoab sector under Simko (1921-22)
i_simko_extended.name_fa: مهاباد، بوکان و میاندوآب در دورهٔ سمیتقو
i_simko_extended.geometry_note: Wikipedia (single source) credits Simko with Mahabad (Sauj Bulaq) from Oct 1921; control of Miandoab/Naghadeh is less certain.

i_kalhor_border_kurds.name: Kalhor-Guran-Sanjabi border Kurds (Kermanshah frontier)
i_kalhor_border_kurds.geometry_note: Iranica: under Davud Khan Kalhor "absolute master of the entire territory between Kermanshah and the Ottoman border", also subjecting Guran and Sanjabi. Counties approximate this border belt.

i_kermanshah_area.name: Kermanshah plain and Hamadan road (Kermanshah, Sahneh, Harsin, Kangavar, Sonqor)
i_kermanshah_area.geometry_note: Core Kermanshah-Sahneh-Bisotun-Harsin corridor that Russian, Ottoman and British forces fought over in 1915-18; the border-belt counties (Qasr-e Shirin etc.) are in i_kalhor_border_kurds.

i_hamadan_area.name: Hamadan province
i_hamadan_area.geometry_note: Modern Hamadan province; Hamadan city and the Hamadan-Kermanshah and Hamadan-Qazvin roads are what was occupied.

i_luristan_pish_e_kuh.name: Luristan (Pish-e Kuh)
i_luristan_pish_e_kuh.geometry_note: Modern Lorestan province. The Pish-e Kuh Lur tribes (Bala Gariveh, Dirakvand, Silakhor, Selseleh, Bayravand...) ranged over this block; the towns of Khorramabad and Borujerd had Qajar governors but the highlands did not obey them.

i_pusht_e_kuh.name: Pusht-e Kuh (Ilam; walis)
i_pusht_e_kuh.geometry_note: Iranica lists Ayvan, Sirvan-Chardavol, Ilam, Darreh Shahr, Mehran and Abdanan as Pusht-e Kuh, with Dehloran sometimes included.

i_bakhtiari.name: Bakhtiari country (Chahar Mahal and eastern Khuzestan)
i_bakhtiari.geometry_note: Summer quarters (yaylaq) in Chahar Mahal and the Zagros crest, winter quarters (qeshlaq) in the Khuzestan piedmont (Masjed Soleyman, Izeh, Lali, Andika, Baghmalek). Fereydan/Fereydunshahr and Semirom fringes and the Khuzestan lowland ranges are excluded.

i_kohgiluyeh_boirahmad.name: Kohgiluyeh, Boir Ahmad and Mamasani
i_kohgiluyeh_boirahmad.geometry_note: Six tribal groups of Kuhgiluya; Boir Ahmad is the largest. Mamasani/Rostam (Fars) joined them under Emamqoli Khan against Reza Shah. The lowland market town Behbahan (Khuzestan) and the Gachsaran/Dogonbadan piedmont fringe are only partly covered; Behbahan is deliberately left out to avoid overlap with the Khuzestan occupation block.

i_qashqai.name: Qashqai range (Fars)
i_qashqai.geometry_note: Qashqai winter quarters in Firuzabad, Farashband, Kazerun and the Gulf-side Qir/Karzin; summer quarters round Semirom, Eqlid, Abadeh and Sepidan. Migration routes crossed Shiraz county. The range was seasonal and overlapped other tribes (Khamseh, Mamasani).

i_mohammerah_core.name: Mohammerah (Khorramshahr) and Abadan island
i_mohammerah_core.geometry_note: Seat of the Muhaysin/Ka'b sheikhs. Modern county boundaries are larger than the 19th-century sheikhdom nucleus.

i_khuzestan_fallahiyeh.name: Fallahiyeh (Shadegan), Hendijan, Mahshahr, Ramshir
i_khuzestan_fallahiyeh.geometry_note: The Ka'b heartland (Fallahiyeh=Shadegan) and the Khaz'al estates granted in 1903 (Fallahiyeh, Hendijan, Deh Molla, Mashur).

i_khuzestan_khazal_ext.name: Northern Khuzestan placed under Khaz'al (1907-24)
i_khuzestan_khazal_ext.name_fa: شمال خوزستان در قلمرو شیخ خزعل
i_khuzestan_khazal_ext.geometry_note: Iranica: from 1907 Khaz'al administered northern Khuzestan; by 1911 "most of the country" was under the sheikh except Dezful and Shushtar. Counties are inferred.

i_lengeh_qawasim.name: Bandar Lengeh and dependencies (Qawasim)
i_lengeh_qawasim.geometry_note: Port of Lengeh and its dependent coast (Charak/Mogh, in Parsian county). Qasimi dependencies on islands (Abu Musa, Tunbs, Sirri) were handled by the frontier researcher.

i_bastak.name: Bastak (hereditary khans)
i_bastak.geometry_note: Hereditary Khans of Bastak governed the Bastak/Irahistan district under the governor of Fars/Lar.

i_larestan.name: Larestan (Lar, Gerash, Evaz, Khonj)
i_larestan.geometry_note: Area ruled by Sayyed Abd al-Hosayn Lari 1909-15; extent between Lar town, Gerash, Khonj and Lamerd inferred from contemporary descriptions.

i_tangestan_dashtestan.name: Tangestan, Dashtestan and Dashti (Bushehr hinterland)
i_tangestan_dashtestan.geometry_note: Tribal districts behind Bushehr; khans of Tangestan (Zair Khidr, Shaikh Hosein Khan of Chah Kutah), Dashtestan and Dashti are the actors.

i_bushehr.name: Bushehr port and county
i_bushehr.geometry_note: Bushehr county includes the port, Reshire and, administratively, Kharg island; Kharg has its own circle region.

i_kharg.name: Kharg island
i_kharg.geometry_note: Small island; circle approximates its outline.

i_basidu.name: Basidu (west tip of Qeshm island)
i_basidu.geometry_note: Station and depot at the west end of Qeshm; British claims never covered the whole island.

i_ashurada.name: Ashurada island (Gorgan Bay)
i_ashurada.geometry_note: Small island group; circle approximates it.

i_omani_lease_bandar_abbas.name: Bandar Abbas, Minab-Khamir coast, Qeshm and Hormuz (Omani lease)
i_omani_lease_bandar_abbas.name_fa: بندرعباس، میناب، خمیر، قشم و هرمز (اجارهٔ عمان)
i_omani_lease_bandar_abbas.geometry_note: Iranica: a coastal strip of about 150 km from Minab in the east to Khamir in the west, plus the islands of Qeshm and Hormuz, and inland about 30 miles in some British accounts. County units over-extend inland; Hormuz is inside Bandar-e Abbas county.

i_spr_garrison_towns.name: South Persia Rifles base at Bandar Abbas (1916-21)
i_spr_garrison_towns.geometry_note: Circle approximation only. Verification: the original single region covered Shiraz, Kerman and Bandar Abbas from March 1916, but Sykes reached Kerman on 12 June 1916 and Shiraz on 11 Nov 1916, so those towns were split into i_spr_kerman and i_spr_shiraz.

i_isfahan_1909.name: Isfahan (Bakhtiari constitutionalists, 1909)
i_isfahan_1909.geometry_note: The two Isfahan keys in the catalog (city-level and surrounding county) are used; their relationship is unclear and may double-cover the same area.

i_iraq_khorramshahr.name: Khorramshahr (Iraqi occupation 1980-82)
i_iraq_khorramshahr.geometry_note: The Iraqi bridgehead covered the city and the eastern bank of the Shatt; the whole county is shown.

i_iraq_abadan.name: Abadan island (siege 1980-81)
i_iraq_abadan.geometry_note: Abadan was besieged but the city and refinery stayed in Iranian hands; Iraqi forces took parts of the north/west of the island and the Bahmanshir bank.

i_iraq_susangerd.name: Susangerd-Bostan-Hoveyzeh plain (Iraqi occupation 1980-82)
i_iraq_susangerd.geometry_note: Iraqi forces held Bostan and parts of Dasht-e Azadegan; exact holdings varied (Iran liberated Bostan 29 Nov-7 Dec 1981, but Iraqi forces still held ground near Susangerd).

i_iraq_west_front.name: Qasr-e Shirin-Sarpol-e Zahab-Gilan-e Gharb-Dehloran (Iraqi occupation 1980-82)
i_iraq_west_front.name_fa: قصرشیرین، سرپل ذهاب، گیلان غرب و دهلران
i_iraq_west_front.geometry_note: Iraq entered 20-40 km deep on this front (Qasr-e Shirin 20 km, Dehloran 30 km according to later accounts); counties overstate the depth.

i_iraq_mehran.name: Mehran
i_iraq_mehran.geometry_note: Mehran changed hands several times (1980, 1986, 1988); the county is shown whole although the occupation was of the town and its approaches.

i_iraq_border_pockets.name: Iraqi-held border pockets after the 1988 ceasefire (to Aug 1990)
i_iraq_border_pockets.name_fa: نوار مرزی در اشغال عراق پس از آتش‌بس
i_iraq_border_pockets.geometry_note: Schematic; do not render as full counties.

i_wwii_soviet_adp.name: Soviet zone of Azerbaijan (ADP area)
i_wwii_soviet_adp.name_fa: آذربایجان در منطقهٔ اشغال شوروی (حکومت پیشه‌وری)
i_wwii_soviet_adp.geometry_note: East and West Azerbaijan (minus the Mahabad-republic counties), Ardabil and Zanjan. Zanjan's inclusion in the ADP is from general accounts; the Democrats' writ in the south of the area (Zanjan, Takab, Miandoab) was thinner and was cut off by the Iranian army before reaching Tabriz.

i_wwii_soviet_north.name: Soviet-occupied north (Gilan, Mazandaran, Golestan, Qazvin)
i_wwii_soviet_north.name_fa: شمال در اشغال شوروی (گیلان، مازندران، گلستان، قزوین، سمنان)
i_wwii_soviet_north.geometry_note: Gilan, Mazandaran and Gorgan are named in the sources; Qazvin (southern outpost of the Soviet line) and Semnan are inferred. Soviet garrisons were concentrated in towns and along the roads; Iranian civil administration continued. (Verification: Semnan province was split out to i_wwii_soviet_semnan because the Soviets left Mashhad/Shahrud/Semnan in March 1946, earlier than the rest.)

i_wwii_soviet_khorasan.name: Soviet-occupied Khorasan (1941-43)
i_wwii_soviet_khorasan.geometry_note: Iranica: Soviet troops took Mashhad and Bojnurd and "occupied all of Khorasan" until winter 1943; the south (Birjand etc.) is not included.

i_wwii_british_zone.name: British-occupied south and west (1941-46)
i_wwii_british_zone.name_fa: جنوب و غرب در اشغال بریتانیا
i_wwii_british_zone.geometry_note: The British entered Khuzestan, Kermanshah and Hamadan in Aug-Sept 1941 and held the Persian Corridor from the Gulf to Hamadan. Paiforce garrisons later reached Isfahan, Shiraz and the Gulf ports, but Fars (Qashqai/Khamseh range, treated separately), Hormozgan and the east are NOT included because British control there was thin or absent. Only a schematic block. Verification: Sanandaj county (IRN2_227) added - British and Soviet columns met at Sanandaj on 30 Aug 1941 and 'southern Kurdistan up to Sanandaj' fell in the British zone (low confidence; the Kurdish-held belt from Mahabad to Saqqez lay between the zones). The wider extent of the British zone (Fars, Isfahan, Kerman, Hormozgan) was not established.

i_wwii_soviet_semnan.name: Soviet-occupied Semnan province (1941-46)
i_wwii_soviet_semnan.geometry_note: Semnan province counties (Shahrud, Damghan, Semnan, Garmsar etc.), split out of i_wwii_soviet_north. Sources say the Soviets held Shahrud and Semnan until March 1946; the extent south to Garmsar is inferred from the Soviet advance to Qazvin/Tehran and the Mashhad road.

i_russian_khoy_1828.name: Khoy (Russian-held pledge, 1828)
i_russian_khoy_1828.geometry_note: Khoy county. Under Turkmenchay Russia evacuated Azerbaijan except Khoy, which it held as a deposit until the indemnity was paid; modern Khoy county is larger than the 1828 district.

i_shiraz_1915.name: Shiraz (pro-German Gendarmerie, 1915-16)
i_shiraz_1915.geometry_note: Circle round Shiraz city; the surrounding Fars countryside was divided among Qashqai, Khamseh and Tangestani forces.

i_zanjan_babi_1850.name: Zanjan town (Babi revolt, 1850-51)
i_zanjan_babi_1850.geometry_note: Circle round Zanjan town; the divided town cannot be mapped more finely.

i_abadan_british_1914.name: Abadan island (British garrison, 1914-18)
i_abadan_british_1914.geometry_note: Abadan county stands in for the island refinery zone; the British perimeter did not cover the whole county.

i_spr_kerman.geometry_note: Circle approximation of the garrison town.

defacto.controller: Iraq
defacto.note: Iraq entered Dehloran, Qasr-e Shirin, Sumar, Naft Shahr, Sar-e Pol-e Zahab and Mousiyan on 12 July 1988 and withdrew from the towns after Iran accepted the ceasefire; but reports in August 1990 say Iraq still held about 2,600 km2 (1,000 sq mi) of Iranian territory, which it began to evacuate on 16-17 Aug 1990 (a UN report of 24 Sept 1990 said withdrawal was almost complete). Locations of the pockets were not identified in sources found. Verification: UNIIMOG's own background says that by end-September 1990 withdrawal to the international boundaries was 'almost complete' with a few locations where forces of each side were still on the wrong side, and that by end-January 1991 Iraq had withdrawn from 23 of 29 disputed positions (Iran from 13 of 17). The pockets were therefore a handful of border positions, not a large contiguous area, and the Aug 1990 '2,600 km2' figure comes from press reports of Saddam Hussein's offer. Record kept at low confidence.

defacto.controller: Iraq vs. Iran (Mehran changed hands several times)
defacto.note: Iraq captured Mehran in the 1980 invasion; Wikipedia ('Battle of Mehran (1986)') calls the May 1986 capture the third time Iraq took it, so Iraqi control before 1986 was not continuous, and the Mehran article says the Iraqis had been driven out by 1982-83. Dates of the first recapture are not established, so the whole span is coded contested (low) instead of the researcher's continuous foreign occupation to June 1982.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Mehran (1986)' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Iraq (II Corps)
defacto.note: Iraq recaptured Mehran on 15-19 May 1986 ("for the third time"); Iran retook the area in Operation Karbala-1 (30 June-3 July 1986) and defeated a Republican Guard counter-attack on 4 July.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Mehran (1986)' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Iraqi forces with the Mojahedin-e Khalq (Operation Forty Stars)
defacto.note: On 18 June 1988 Iraq and the MEK crushed two Iranian divisions and seized Mehran; Iraqi regulars left after three days and the MEK stayed. Wikipedia says Iran retook Mehran in Operation Mersad (26 July); the end date is uncertain.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Operation Forty Stars' and 'Operation Mersad' (cross-check; dates of Mehran 1988 uncertain)

defacto.controller: Iraq
defacto.note: Iraqi forces held Bostan and parts of the Dasht-e Azadegan plain (the Susangerd salient). Iran relieved a siege of Susangerd in Nov 1980 and recaptured Bostan and 70 villages on 29 Nov-7 Dec 1981 (Operation Tariq al-Quds); the rest was cleared by June 1982. Holdings varied by month. Verification (Iranica 'Iraq vii'): after Fath ol-Mobin (22 March 1982, Shush-Dezful) and the 22 March offensive north of Bostan, the stage of 24 April-12 May 1982 'drove the Iraqi troops back to Khorramshahr from the Ahvaz-Susangird area'; the end is therefore moved from 1982-06 (the date of Iraq's general withdrawal announcement) to 1982-05. Khorramshahr itself (separate record) fell on 24-25 May.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Operation Tariq al-Quds' and 'Liberation of Susangerd' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Iraq vii. Iran-Iraq War' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iraq-vii-iran-iraq-war/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Iraq vii. Iran-Iraq War' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iraq-vii-iran-iraq-war/) [read directly: spring 1982 offensives]

defacto.controller: Iraq
defacto.note: Iraq took Qasr-e Shirin on the first days of the invasion and advanced on the Kermanshah and Ilam fronts (Sar-e Pol-e Zahab, Gilan-e Gharb, Musian/Dehloran); the central-front lines were pushed back in Dec 1981-Jan 1982 and Iraq announced its withdrawal on 20 June 1982. Town-by-town dates are not established here.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Iraq vii. Iran-Iraq War' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iraq-vii-iran-iraq-war/)
Wikipedia, 'Tawakalna ala Allah Operations' (cross-check; Iraqi entry to Dehloran/Qasr-e Shirin 12 July 1988)

defacto.controller: Bakhtiari constitutionalist khans (Samsam al-Saltaneh, Sardar As'ad)
defacto.note: Bakhtiari forces took Isfahan in early 1909 and, with Sardar As'ad (who entered the city on 14 May 1909 per Iranica), marched on Tehran with the Gilan force, which fell on 13 July 1909. Dates are approximate.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Baḵtīārī' articles incl. 'Baḵtīārī tribe', 'Esfandīār Khan', 'Baktiari ii' (iranicaonline.org) [search extracts]

defacto.controller: Kalhor chiefs (Davud Khan, killed 1912 fighting for Salar al-Dowleh; his successor Abbas Khan), with Guran and Sanjabi subordinate
defacto.note: Iranica: Davud Khan Kalhor, who 'ruled the tribe in the early 1900s', started as a peddler and made himself 'the absolute master of the entire territory between Kermanshah and the Ottoman border', also subjugating the Guran and Sanjabi; he held the Qajar title Sardar-e Mozaffar and governed the Kalhor district. He was killed fighting for Salar al-Dowleh (1911 per British records and Wikipedia; 1912 per Iranica) and his successor Abbas Khan was imprisoned by Reza Shah in 1926. CORRECTION: the researcher's 1800 start is dropped. Before c.1900 the Kalhor were one of several tribes inside the province of Kermanshah, governed from the city by Qajar princes (Kalhor and Zangana levies served those governors, e.g. against the Bakhtiari in 1830), with no autonomous Kalhor ruler; those years are left as direct. The exact start of Davud Khan's ascendancy (c.1900) is approximate.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kalhor' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kalhor/) [search extract]
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kermanshah iv. History to 1953' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kermanshah-04-history-to-1953/)
Wikipedia, 'Kalhor (tribe)' (cross-check; Qajar-era role of the Kalhor and Zangana under the governors of Kermanshah)

defacto.controller: Salar al-Dowleh (Abolfath Mirza) with Kalhor, Jaf, Sanjabi and Lur followers vs. Bakhtiari/government forces
defacto.note: Mohammad Ali Shah's brother occupied Sanandaj by 17 July 1911, seized Kermanshah (given up to plunder) and, per Wikipedia, Hamadan; he marched on Tehran, won a first battle near Malayer and was decisively beaten near Saveh by Amir Mofakham Bakhtiari (his Kalhor ally Davud Khan died in this campaign: 1911 per the British records and Wikipedia, 1912 per Iranica). The revolt did not end there: he remained in the Kermanshah-Kurdistan area until Farman Farma's 1912 expedition (Persian Gulf Administration Report 1911-14: 'In July Salar-ed-Dowleh fled from Kermanshah, on the arrival of Farman Farma ... and left for Luristan and Kurdistan'), so the end is moved from Dec 1911 to July 1912. Control of each town in between is not established; status stays contested.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kermanshah iv. History to 1953' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kermanshah-04-history-to-1953/)
Persian Gulf Political Residency, Administration Report 1911-1914 (IOR/L/PS), via Qatar Digital Library [search extract: Salar-ed-Dowleh fled from Kermanshah in July on Farman Farma's arrival]

defacto.controller: Committee for the Defence of Iran's Independence / National (Provisional) Government of Kermanshah under Nezam al-Saltaneh Mafi, backed by German and Ottoman agents
defacto.note: Nationalists left Tehran for Qom (Nov 1915) and set up an anti-Allied government at Kermanshah; Ottoman and German forces occupied the city in 1915-16. The government fell back before the Russian entry on 26 Feb 1916.
sources: University of Edinburgh thesis abstract, 'Muhajirat and the National Government of Kermanshah, 1915-1917' (era.ed.ac.uk) [search extract]
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kermanshah iv. History to 1953' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kermanshah-04-history-to-1953/)

defacto.controller: Imperial Russian Caucasian Cavalry Corps (Gen. Baratov)
defacto.note: Russian forces broke through at Sahneh (22 Feb), took Bisotun (24 Feb) and entered Kermanshah on 26 Feb 1916; the Ottoman XIII Corps (Ali Ihsan) retook it on 2 July 1916.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Kermanshah operation' (cross-check; Russian entry to Kermanshah 26 Feb 1916)
Wikipedia, 'Persian campaign (World War I)' (cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations)

defacto.controller: Ottoman Empire (XIII Corps, Ali Ihsan) and German officers, with the returned Persian nationalist government
defacto.note: The Ottomans held Kermanshah from 2 July 1916 until their retreat after the fall of Baghdad (11 March 1917); the exact evacuation date is not established. Verification: Wikipedia ('Battle of Khanaqin') says the Russians occupied Khanaqin after Ali Ihsan was recalled to Baghdad in Feb 1917, so the Ottoman hold on Kermanshah ended between Feb and mid-March 1917; the exact date remains unknown.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Persian campaign (World War I)' (cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kermanshah iv. History to 1953' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kermanshah-04-history-to-1953/)
Wikipedia, 'Battle of Khanaqin' (cross-check; Ali Ihsan recalled Feb 1917, Russians occupy Khanaqin)

defacto.controller: Imperial Russia (Baratov's remaining troops, disintegrating after the revolution)
defacto.note: After the Ottoman retreat Russian forces re-entered the Kermanshah area; most Russian troops left Persia between December 1917 and March 1918, a few under Baratov passing into British service. Dates low-confidence.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Russia i. Russo-Iranian Relations up to the Bolshevik Revolution' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/russia-i-relations/)
Wikipedia, 'Persian campaign (World War I)' (cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations)

defacto.controller: British (Dunsterforce lines of communication, then Norperforce)
defacto.note: The British held the Mesopotamia-Kermanshah-Hamadan-Qazvin-Anzali road line; Dunsterville reached Hamadan in Feb 1918. The garrisons were progressively reduced; Norperforce withdrew on 21 April 1921. Persian civil authority continued.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Dunsterforce' (cross-check)
FIBIS wiki, 'Norperforce' (wiki.fibis.org/w/Norperforce)

defacto.controller: Britain (East India Company/Bombay Marine; Residency moved from Bushehr to Kharg)
defacto.note: Occupied on 19 June 1838 in response to Mohammad Shah's siege of Herat; the Persians lifted the siege on 9 Sept 1838 but, "owing to the shifty character of their subsequent diplomacy", the island was not evacuated until March 1842.
sources: Qatar Digital Library, 'A Strategic Position: British Seizures of the Island of Kharg' and Lorimer, Gazetteer (occupation 19 June 1838 - March 1842) [search extracts]

defacto.controller: Britain (naval force; island garrisoned through the Anglo-Persian War)
defacto.note: Occupied 4 Dec 1856; Iranica: held until spring 1858 although the main forces left in 1857.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Anglo-Persian War (1856-57)' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/anglo-persian-war-1856-57/)

defacto.controller: Ka'b sheikhs of Fallahiyeh, then Khaz'al (decrees of 1903 granting Fallahiyeh, Hendijan, Deh Molla and Mashur as perpetual holdings)
defacto.note: The Ka'b heartland and the coastal lands behind Mohammerah were held by Arab sheikhs acknowledging the shah. Pre-1897 holdings and rulers are only loosely characterised here.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Ḵazʿal Khan' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kazal-khan/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'ʿArab iv. Arab tribes of Iran' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/arab-iv/)

defacto.controller: Sheikh Khaz'al (administrator of northern Khuzestan from 1907)
defacto.note: Sardar Mokarram (later Nezam al-Saltaneh) placed Khaz'al in charge of northern Khuzestan in 1907; by 1911 the governorship "does not confer any great powers, most of the country being under the rule of the Shaikh" with only Dezful and Shushtar outside his control.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Ḵazʿal Khan' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kazal-khan/)

defacto.controller: Khans of Boir Ahmad (Garmsir/Sardsir), the Noi and other Kuhgiluya khans; Mamasani chief Emamqoli Khan
defacto.note: The tribal khans fell foul of the Qajars (Mohammad-Taher Khan blinded c.1800) but generally ruled their districts under nominal Qajar suzerainty with the Fars governor's backing at times. Tang-e Tamradi (Aug 1930) was a major tribal defeat of Reza Shah's army.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Boir Aḥmadī' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/boir-ahmadi/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fars-iv/)

defacto.controller: Boir Ahmad / Kohgiluyeh / Mamasani khans vs. Reza Shah's army
defacto.note: After the Tamradi defeat (heavy losses - Iranica Boir Ahmadi: "said to have exceeded 1,000 casualties"; Fars iv gives about 400 killed; Aug 1930) the khans eventually surrendered and were executed in 1932; a military government then imposed order for the next decade.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Boir Aḥmadī' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/boir-ahmadi/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fars-iv/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Boir Aḥmadī' (casualty figure)

defacto.controller: Boir Ahmad and Kohgiluyeh khans (tribal political system "rebounded with amazing vigor")
defacto.note: After Reza Shah's abdication central authority collapsed locally and tribal politics revived. In 1962-63 two khans resisted land reform, ambushed government forces at Tang-e Gochestan/Gachina Pass and were crushed in June 1963; thereafter the area was under tight security-force control.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Boir Aḥmadī' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/boir-ahmadi/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fars-iv/)

defacto.controller: Kurdish groups (KDPI, Komala, local councils) vs. the Islamic Republic
defacto.note: Kurdish forces took the towns and garrisons of Paveh and Marivan region in March 1979; the army retook Paveh in the August 1979 offensive and mountain areas remained insurgent until 1983-84.
sources: Wikipedia, '1979 Kurdish rebellion in Iran' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qāsemlu, ʿAbd-al-Raḥmān' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qasemlu/)

defacto.controller: Sayyed Abd al-Hosayn Lari (Najafi Lari), a pro-constitution mujtahid
defacto.note: In 1909 he proclaimed a revolt, issued his own postage stamps (in use March-May 1909) and, per Iranica, "ruled Larestan until the spring of 1915", when the governor-general of Fars sent Habib-Allah Khan Qavam al-Molk to pacify it. Lorimer-based accounts have him driven from Lar and returning in August 1909 and later deported to Shiraz; continuity of control is uncertain.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv' (Sayyed ʿAbd-al-Ḥosayn Lārī 1909-spring 1915) [search extract]
Lorimer-based extract quoted by philatelic sources: Lari's stamps in use March-May 1909; re-entered Lar August 1909 (rpsl.org.uk / qdl.qa 'Administration Reports 1905-10') [search extract]

defacto.controller: Qawasim (Qasimi) sheikhs of Lengeh (Sheikh Qazib ibn Rashid last)
defacto.note: The Qasimi sheikh administered Lengeh for the Persian government from about 1789 as revenue collector under the governor of Bastak/Fars. In Feb 1887 Persia created the "Gulf Ports" governorate; in September 1887 the Qasimi governorship was dissolved, Sheikh Qazib was arrested and a Persian garrison landed; Sheikh Mohammad ibn Khalifa briefly seized Lengeh in 1898-99 before Ahmad Khan Daryabeigi retook it in March 1899.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bandar-e Lenga' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/bandar-e-lenga/) and 'Great Britain iii'/'Abu Musa' search extracts on 1887
Wikipedia, 'Bandar Lengeh' (cross-check; 1887-88 takeover, 1898-99 interlude)

defacto.controller: Pish-e Kuh Lur tribes under their own chiefs (Qajar governor-general sat at Khorramabad)
defacto.note: The wali dynasty of Luristan was overthrown in 1796 and replaced at Khorramabad by a governor-general, but the highland tribes kept their own organisation; the Pish-e Kuh was "largely outside control" until Reza Khan's army went in (April 1921 onward).
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Pošt-e Kuh' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/post-e-kuh/)
Wikipedia, 'Luri tribal insurgency in Pahlavi Iran' (cross-check; Reza Khan's Luristan campaigns 1921-33)

defacto.controller: Lur tribes vs. Reza Khan's army
defacto.note: The army deployed to Luristan in April 1921, took Borujerd (Oct 1923) and Khorramabad (Nov 1923), met a major revolt in May 1924 and the last major engagement in 1926. Wikipedia says direct control came in 1928; Iranica says war dragged on to 1933 but migration was banned from 1929.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Luri tribal insurgency in Pahlavi Iran' (cross-check; Reza Khan's Luristan campaigns 1921-33)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Luristan' articles (iranicaonline.org), search extract: army in Luristan 1922, war to 1933, migration banned from 1929

defacto.controller: Mukri khans/emirs of Mukriyan as Qajar-appointed hereditary governors (Sauj Bulaq/Mahabad)
defacto.note: Mukriyan, south of Lake Urmia, was ruled by hereditary Mokri khans who served the Qajars as governors of Savojbolagh (Sayf al-Din Khan, d. 1891/2, held the post several times; his son Hosein Khan was killed in the Ottoman attack of 1914). Their power was eroded after Ubeydullah's 1880 invasion: the Qajar state built the Savujbulagh garrison in 1883 (Sayadi 2019: 'a manifestation of the exclusion of the Mukris from the Qajar political power structure'), so 1883 replaces the former 1880-10 placeholder. Not independently dated to the month; some accounts keep Mokri influence into the 1910s.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mukriyan' (cross-check; weak on Qajar-period chronology)

Sayadi, N., 'Architecture of Exclusion: The Savujbulagh-i Mukri Garrison, Border-Making, and the Transformation of the Ottoman-Qajar Frontier' (2019; Archnet) [search extract: garrison 1883 to c.1910s]
Wikipedia, 'Aziz Khan Mokri' (cross-check; Sayf al-Din Khan and Hosein Khan as governors of Savojbolagh)

defacto.controller: Local Kurdish chiefs and the Society for the Revival of Kurdistan (Komala-i Jiyanewey Kurdistan, 1942) under Qazi Muhammad; Soviet zone
defacto.note: After the Iranian army collapsed in Aug-Sept 1941 Kurdish leaders returned and rearmed; Soviet forces held the zone to the north and the Iranian gendarmerie and army were driven out of the Mahabad area. Qazi Muhammad led the Komala (1942) and the KDP (founded Sept 1945). Per British-zone accounts, southern Kurdistan up to Sanandaj was under British occupation, while the Kurdish-held belt from Mahabad to Saqqez lay between the two zones; by 1945 the Iranian government effectively controlled Kurdish areas only south of the Saqqez-Baneh-Sardasht line. Start date approximate.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Republic of Mahabad' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Azarbaijan v. History from 1941 to 1947' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/azerbaijan-v/)
Kurdistan Chronicle, 'Soviet Union's Politics Toward the Iranian Kurds' (kurdistanchronicle.com/babat/2718) [search extract on zones]

defacto.controller: Republic of Mahabad (Qazi Muhammad, president)
defacto.note: Iranica ('Azarbaijan v') has Qazi Muhammad inaugurating the Kurdish Republic at Mahabad on 15 December 1945; Wikipedia gives 22 Jan 1946 for the formal proclamation and presidency. Because the question here is when a rival administration actually replaced Tehran's, 15 Dec 1945 is used (the Jan 1946 proclamation is event i_ev_mahabad_republic_1946). Territory: Mahabad, Bukan, Naghadeh, Piranshahr and Oshnavieh (Sardasht usually added); the republic claimed but did not hold Urmia, Khoy and Salmas. After the Soviets left (May 1946) it was isolated; Iranian troops entered Mahabad on 15-17 Dec 1946.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Azarbaijan v. History from 1941 to 1947' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/azerbaijan-v/)
Wikipedia, 'Republic of Mahabad' (cross-check)
Wikipedia, 'Iran crisis of 1946' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: KDPI and allied Kurdish councils at Mahabad
defacto.note: Mahabad stayed in Kurdish hands from early March 1979 (KDPI held the military base) until the army, using F-4s and over 100 tanks, took it on 3 Sept 1979; Sardasht, Bukan and Piranshahr fell on 4-6 Sept. Start is approximate (Feb-Mar 1979).
sources: Wikipedia, '1979 Kurdish rebellion in Iran' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qāsemlu, ʿAbd-al-Raḥmān' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qasemlu/)

defacto.controller: KDPI peshmerga vs. IRGC and army
defacto.note: Qasemlu returned to Mahabad on 20 Oct 1979 as rebels retook the town; in Nov 1979 Kurds held most roads and rural areas. After the spring 1980 government offensive retook the cities, the KDPI controlled "a major portion of Iranian Kurdistan, excluding the towns" in 1981-82; IRGC and Iranian forces drove them out in 1982-83 and the KDPI left for Iraq by early 1984.
sources: Wikipedia, '1979 Kurdish rebellion in Iran' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qāsemlu, ʿAbd-al-Raḥmān' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qasemlu/)

defacto.controller: Nader Mirza Afshar (grandson of Nader Shah), backed by the Afghan rulers of Herat
defacto.note: After Agha Mohammad Khan's death (1797) Nader Mirza returned to Mashhad and styled himself sovereign of Khorasan. Fath-Ali Shah failed in 1799 and 1801, besieged the city in 1802 and Mohammad-Vali Mirza took it in early 1803; Nader was blinded and executed in Tehran. Reach beyond the Mashhad district is not established.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Khorasan xi. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/khorasan-xi-history-in-the-qajar-and-pahlavi-periods/)

Wikipedia, 'Nader Mirza Afshar' (cross-check only)

defacto.controller: Mohammad-Hasan Khan Salar (son of Asaf al-Dowleh) with local khans and ulama
defacto.note: Mashhad rose on 25 Aug 1848, just before Mohammad Shah's death in early September, and held out against Hamza Mirza and then Sultan Morad Mirza; besieged from June 1849, it surrendered on 13 or 23 March 1850. Salar was executed on 29 April 1850. Iranica dates the whole revolt c.1847-51; the day-level chronology comes from Wikipedia only.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Khorasan xi. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/khorasan-xi-history-in-the-qajar-and-pahlavi-periods/)
Wikipedia, 'Revolt of Hasan Khan Salar' (cross-check; the only source consulted giving the 1848-50 day-level chronology)

defacto.controller: Ka'b / Muhaysin sheikhs of Mohammerah (Hajji Jabir) under Qajar suzerainty with Ottoman claims
defacto.note: The Ka'b and later Muhaysin sheikhs "were for two centuries the most powerful chieftains of south-western Persia". Muhammara's allegiance shifted between Persia and the Ottomans.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'ʿArab iv. Arab tribes of Iran' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/arab-iv/)
Wikipedia, 'Khorramshahr' (cross-check; alternately claimed and occupied by Persia and Turkey until the 1847 Treaty of Erzurum)

defacto.controller: Ottoman Baghdad (Ali Rida Pasha) vs. Persia over the Muhaysin sheikhdom
defacto.note: In 1837 Ali Rida Pasha captured and destroyed Muhammara and the Ka'b paid homage to the Ottomans; the town was "alternately claimed and occupied" until the Second Treaty of Erzurum (31 May 1847), Article II, ceded Mohammerah and Khizr island to Persia. Duration of the Ottoman occupation is not established.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ali Rıza Pasha (governor of Baghdad)' (cross-check; 1837 capture of Muhammara)
Wikipedia, 'Khorramshahr' (cross-check; alternately claimed and occupied by Persia and Turkey until the 1847 Treaty of Erzurum)

defacto.controller: Muhaysin sheikhs of Mohammerah (Hajji Jabir, Sheikh Thamer, Sheikh Yusuf)
defacto.note: After Erzurum the sheikhs remained semi-autonomous under Persian suzerainty.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'ʿArab iv. Arab tribes of Iran' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/arab-iv/)

defacto.controller: Britain (Indian Army expeditionary force, Gen. Outram)
defacto.note: Mohammerah fell on 26-27 March 1857 after naval bombardment; the flotilla reached Ahvaz on 1 April; hostilities ceased about 4 April and the Treaty of Paris was ratified on 2 May. British forces left in mid-1857 (the main force sailed for India in May-June because of the Mutiny); exact evacuation date not established.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Anglo-Persian War (1856-57)' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/anglo-persian-war-1856-57/)
Wikipedia, 'Anglo-Persian War' (cross-check; Bushehr evacuated Oct 1857)

defacto.controller: Muhaysin sheikhs; Sheikh Khaz'al Khan (sheikh from June 1897)
defacto.note: Khaz'al succeeded his assassinated brother Mazal in June 1897, was recognised as Sardar Arfa' (1902), enjoyed British protection (assurances 1899-1908; KCIE 1910/1917) and ruled a "semi-independent realm". On 6 Dec 1924 he submitted to Reza Khan at Ahvaz; he was seized on 18 April 1925 and held in Tehran until his death (27 May 1936). The 1857-97 part of this span is only loosely characterised.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Ḵazʿal Khan' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kazal-khan/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'ʿArab iv. Arab tribes of Iran' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/arab-iv/)

defacto.controller: Sultanate of Muscat and Oman (Al Bu Sa'id) under lease from the Qajar shahs
defacto.note: Under a Persian firman of 1793/94 the Sultan administered Bandar Abbas, the Minab-Khamir coastal strip and the islands of Qeshm and Hormuz for 75 years (garrison of 120 Nubians and 80 Arabs in 1811). Mulla Hosein of Qeshm seized Bandar Abbas after 1804; the Qasimi and the Bombay Marine contested Qeshm c.1806-10. A 1855 accord limited the lease to 20 years at 16,000 tomans a year; the Qajars regained the port in October 1868 amid dynastic trouble in Muscat.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bandar-e ʿAbbās i. The City' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/bandar-e-abbasi/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qešm Island' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qeshm-island/)
Qatar Digital Library, 'No Place Equal to It: The Omani Lease of Bandar Abbas' parts 1-2 (qdl.qa) [search extract]

defacto.controller: Ottoman Empire (troops on the orders of the vali of Baghdad, with Sunni Kurdish tribes)
defacto.note: The Ottomans began occupying Persian frontier districts on 23 May 1906 (Behik in Baradost), taking Dasht, Mergever and parts of Sardasht, Bana, Ganjachin and Baradost; Mergever was occupied again on 3 Aug 1907. Pressure by Russia and Britain pushed them back around 1911-12; the withdrawal was incomplete and intermittent. End date is approximate.

defacto.controller: Col. Mohammad-Taqi Khan Pesyan, commander of the Khorasan Gendarmerie, at Mashhad
defacto.note: Pesyan was made military governor-general by the post-coup government on 2-3 April 1921. After Qavam al-Saltaneh became premier (late May) and sent Najd al-Saltaneh as governor, Pesyan resumed full control in July and defied Tehran until killed fighting Kurdish forces under Sardar Mo'azzaz Bojnurdi at Quchan on 3 Oct 1921. Wikipedia counts the 'Autonomous Government of Khorasan' from 2 April; the rebel phase is dated here from c. June-July.

defacto.controller: Valis of Pusht-e Kuh (hereditary Faili Lur 'Vali dynasty': Hoseynqoli Khan Abu Qaddara to c.1900-01, then his son Gholam-Reza Khan, titled Sarim al-Saltaneh/Sardar Ashrafi)
defacto.note: After 1796 the wali family withdrew from Khorramabad to Pusht-e Kuh, where 'quasi-autonomous governors (wali)' ruled until about 1929 (Iranica). Wali names confirmed: Hoseynqoli Khan Abu Qaddara, succeeded around 1900-01 by his son Gholam-Reza Khan, who 'only tacitly acknowledged his vassal status to the Qajars with annual tribute' (hence indirect), held the rank of major-general and fled to Baghdad with his valuables in 1928-29 rather than accept Reza Shah's invitation to Tehran; he died in Baghdad in 1939. The researcher's alternative account (Vali defeated and fleeing to Iraq with Simko in 1922) is contradicted by this chronology and is dropped.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Pošt-e Kuh' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/post-e-kuh/)

defacto.controller: Khozeimeh 'Alam amirs of Qa'enat (Mir 'Alam Khan Heshmat al-Molk; Amir Esma'il Shawkat al-Molk, to 1904; Amir Mohammad Ebrahim Shawkat al-Molk, governor 1904-1924, then his two nephews, incl. Amir Ma'soum Khan, 'the last ruling amir')
defacto.note: Hereditary local rulers of Birjand/Qa'en acknowledged the Qajars and acted as their governors (Iranica: 'in practice the administration of large parts of [Khorasan] was in the hands of local tribal khans', among them the Khozeima 'Alam of Birjand and the Qa'enat). Correction: Shawkat al-Molk was governor 1904-1924, not 'to the 1930s'; he resigned in 1924 handing power to two nephews and moved to Tehran, was governor of Fars 1937 and returned to Birjand in 1942 (d. 1944). The family's hereditary hold ended sometime in the 1930s; no source gives a date, so 1935 is a marker only. Mirza Rafi' Khan's rebellion from the citadel of Furg (1850s) was put down.

defacto.controller: Qashqai ilkhanis (Jani Khan, ilkhani from 1818/19; Mohammad-Ali Khan 1823-52; Mohammad-Qoli Khan 1852-67/8; Esmail Khan Soulat al-Dowleh from 1904)
defacto.note: The Qashqai ilkhanate controlled Fars' grazing lands and routes, bowing to the shah at times (Mohammad-Ali Khan was held at court in 1836) and dominating Fars during the weak central rule of 1909-21 (1911 civil war with the Qavami; anti-British rising in 1918; Soulat al-Dowleh reinstated as ilkhani by Mosaddeq in late 1920). CORRECTION: the record ended 1929-03, but Iranica says that in 1926 Soulat al-Dowleh and Nasser Khan were summoned to Tehran as deputies and became virtual prisoners, and 'military governors were assigned to the various Qashqai tribes' with conscription and a new tax system - i.e. direct rule 1926-29. Highly variable autonomy; treated as a single phase.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qašqāʾi tribal confederacy i. History' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qasqai-tribal-confederacy-i/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fars-iv/)

defacto.controller: Qashqai (Soulat al-Dowleh, Nasser Khan, Khosrow Khan) and allied tribes vs. Reza Shah
defacto.note: The 1929 rising began in spring (the Khamseh Baharlu drove officials out of Darab at the end of April and took Fasa on 9 May); on 4 June the Qashqai closed the Bushehr road and then the Isfahan road, isolating Shiraz, which was under siege by mid-June; on 10 July the government flew Soulat al-Dowleh from prison to Shiraz to negotiate; the Khamseh occupied the eastern towns and the Baharlu reached the Kerman frontier; by summer the rebels held 'the whole province of Fars' outside the cities (Iranica 'Fars iv'). It ended with the August 1929 truce and amnesty. CORRECTION: the record previously ran to 1933 as 'contested'; the 1929 truce withdrew the military governors, and the 1932 rebellion 'in vain' is not documented as holding territory (see the next record).
sources: Wikipedia, 'Persian tribal uprisings of 1929' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qašqāʾi tribal confederacy i. History' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qasqai-tribal-confederacy-i/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fars-iv/)

Wikipedia, 'Persian tribal uprisings of 1929' (cross-check; summarising the British Persian Gulf Administration Reports 1926-38: Darab end April, Fasa 9 May, roads closed 4 June, Soulat released 10 July)

defacto.controller: Qashqai ilkhani family (Soulat al-Dowleh, Nasser Khan, Khosrow Khan), reinstated in the Majles after the truce
defacto.note: After the 1929 truce Soulat al-Dowleh and Nasser Khan were reinstated as deputies, the military governors were withdrawn from tribal territory and a general amnesty was declared (Iranica). The Qashqai rebelled again in 1932 'but in vain', Soulat al-Dowleh died in prison in 1933 and the army then cut the migration routes; direct control followed. Low confidence on both ends.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qašqāʾi tribal confederacy i. History' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qasqai-tribal-confederacy-i/)

defacto.controller: Qashqai under Nasser Khan (ilkhani) and Khosrow Khan, with German agent Schulze-Holthus from 1942
defacto.note: After Reza Shah's abdication (16 Sept 1941) the brothers escaped from Tehran, proclaimed themselves ilkhani and resumed nomadism; Persian troops were dispatched only in spring 1943 and heavy fighting followed (200+ soldiers killed at Semirom, 1943).
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qašqāʾi tribal confederacy i. History' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qasqai-tribal-confederacy-i/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fars-iv/)

defacto.controller: Qashqai (Nasser Khan) under a treaty granting autonomy and arms in exchange for army garrisons
defacto.note: The 1943-44 agreement left the tribes armed and largely self-governing while allowing garrisons; the confederacy enjoyed "almost complete autonomy" through 1945-53.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qašqāʾi tribal confederacy i. History' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qasqai-tribal-confederacy-i/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fars-iv/)

defacto.controller: Southern tribes' "Sa'adun"/South Resistance movement vs. the Qavam government
defacto.note: In September 1946 Nasser Khan convened a conference of the southern tribes which rose against Qavam; the Qashqai took Kazerun and Abadeh and broke through Shiraz's outer defences until Qavam dismissed the Tudeh ministers and met demands (Oct 1946). Duration about one to one and a half months.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qašqāʾi tribal confederacy i. History' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qasqai-tribal-confederacy-i/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fars-iv/)

defacto.controller: Qashqai (Four Brothers: Nasser, Malek-Mansur, Mohammad-Hosein, Khosrow Khan)
defacto.note: Near-complete autonomy continued until the 1953 coup; in 1954 the brothers were exiled and their property confiscated.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qašqāʾi tribal confederacy i. History' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qasqai-tribal-confederacy-i/)

defacto.controller: Qashqai insurgents (Khosrow Khan Qashqai) vs. IRGC
defacto.note: After an attempt to arrest Khosrow Khan in June 1980, Qashqai insurgents "defied the central government" for two years from camps in the mountains until a night attack by the Revolutionary Guards in April 1982; Khosrow Khan was executed on 8 Oct 1982. This was a mobile insurgency, not territorial control; included at low confidence. Verification: this is the weakest record in the file - a mobile insurgency from mountain camps, not control of the Qashqai counties; the IRGC held the towns and roads. Kept at low confidence rather than deleted; the opposite-error risk (central control actually direct) is real.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qašqāʾi tribal confederacy i. History' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qasqai-tribal-confederacy-i/)

defacto.controller: British North Persia Force (Norperforce)
defacto.note: Formed 16 Sept 1918 from Dunsterforce remnants with its HQ at Qazvin, the main body at Manjil and a battalion at Zanjan; about 6,000 men in 1918, 3,600 by 26 Oct 1920; completely withdrawn into Mesopotamia on 21 April 1921, leaving its arms to the Persian Cossacks. Persian administration continued.
sources: FIBIS wiki, 'Norperforce' (wiki.fibis.org/w/Norperforce)
Wikipedia, 'Dunsterforce' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Za'faranlu Kurdish ilkhanis of Quchan (e.g. Reza-Qoli Khan, defeated by Abbas Mirza in 1832; Sam Khan)
defacto.note: Kurdish khans held the Quchan marches as hereditary governors, fielding thousands of horsemen and acknowledging the shah only intermittently. Reza Khan's bombing of Bojnurd (18 May 1925) opened the end of the Kurdish ilkhani system; end date is therefore a convenience marker, not a precise date for Quchan. Abbas Mirza razed the Quchan fortress and exiled Reza-Qoli Khan after the 1832 battle (13,000 Kurds against 19,000 men); Iranica nonetheless says the Za'faranlu kept their tribal structure and ilkhani leadership throughout the Qajar era (Sam Khan fought for the shah against Salar and at Herat), and that Chenaran and Darreh Gaz were 'from time to time' under the governor of Khorasan's direct rule. So 'indirect' is retained, with brief direct episodes.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Khorasan xvii. The Kurdish Communities of Khorasan' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/khorasan-xvii-the-kurdish-communities-of-khorasan/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Khorasan xi. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/khorasan-xi-history-in-the-qajar-and-pahlavi-periods/)

defacto.controller: Imperial Russian army (Gen. Paskevich)
defacto.note: Khoy was held as a deposit until the whole indemnity was paid. Kinneir's letters show the Russians still in Khoy on 14 and 25 Aug 1828 (he suspected they hoped to occupy it indefinitely), and his dispatch of 26 Nov 1828 reports the withdrawal from Khoy in exchange for a large Persian payment (with a 100,000-toman gift from Paskevich on receipt). End set to Nov 1828 (low); the start month is not established (after the fall of Tabriz on 13 Oct 1827).
sources: Kinneir, letters of 14 and 25 Aug 1828 (IOR/L/PS/9/71/288-289) and Dispatch 121 of 26 Nov 1828 (IOR/L/PS/9/71/304), Qatar Digital Library (qdl.qa, vdc_100038378586.0x000496, 0x000497, 0x0004a6)

defacto.controller: Imperial Russian army (Gen. Paskevich)
defacto.note: Tabriz was taken on 13 Oct 1827, Urmia on 28 Jan 1828 and Ardabil on 8 Feb 1828. Turkmenchay (22 Feb 1828) tied evacuation to indemnity instalments. Kinneir reported on 12 March 1828 that he had negotiated 'the immediate evacuation of Azerbijan, with the exception of Khoee' and that the Russians were 'duly preparing to withdraw'; Paskevich left Tabriz in March. The end is therefore set at April 1828 (low); Khoy is handled in i_russian_khoy_1828.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Treaty of Turkmenchay' and 'Russo-Persian War (1826-1828)' (cross-check; Tabriz 13 Oct 1827, Urmia 28 Jan 1828, Ardabil 8 Feb 1828)

defacto.controller: Hasan Khan Salar and his Turkmen/Kurdish/local allies
defacto.note: After Hamza Mirza withdrew, Salar dominated most of Khorasan; the government counter-offensive retook Sabzevar (9 March 1849) and Neyshabur (21 March 1849). Start date is approximate (late summer/autumn 1848).
sources: Wikipedia, 'Revolt of Hasan Khan Salar' (cross-check; the only source consulted giving the 1848-50 day-level chronology)

defacto.controller: Ardalan valis of Senneh (Sanandaj); last wali Amanollah Khan Ardalan
defacto.note: The Ardalan family ruled Kurdistan as hereditary vali under the Qajars. In 1284/1867-68 Naser al-Din Shah ended the vilayet's special status and appointed his uncle Farhad Mirza Mo'tamed al-Dowleh governor of the province of Kurdistan.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Banī Ardalān' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/bani-ardalan-a-kurdish-tribe-of-northwestern-iran-now-dispersed-in-sanandaj-senna-and-surrounding-villages/) [search extract]
Wikipedia, 'Ardalan' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Kurdish groups (KDPI, Komala, local councils) vs. the Islamic Republic (army, IRGC)
defacto.note: Kurdish groups seized garrisons in Sanandaj (17-19 March 1979), Saqqez, Marivan and Paveh; Khomeini declared jihad on 17 Aug 1979 and the government retook Sanandaj and Saqqez by early September. In 1981-82 the Kurds held most of the countryside outside the towns; IRGC pushed them out in 1982-83 and the KDPI withdrew to Iraq by early 1984 (Komala persisted slightly longer). Towns and countryside flipped repeatedly; the whole span is coded contested.
sources: Wikipedia, '1979 Kurdish rebellion in Iran' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qāsemlu, ʿAbd-al-Raḥmān' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qasemlu/)

defacto.controller: Shahsevan tribal khans ("the time of the independent khans")
defacto.note: Russia closed the Moghan frontier to the Shahsevan in 1884 and between 1884 and 1922 the Shahsevan operated with minimal central authority. They were among the first major tribes pacified and disarmed by Reza Khan's army in winter-spring 1922-23. Status before 1884 (Qajar-appointed governors with tribal chiefs) is not recorded here. Verification (Iranica 'Shahsevan'): 'virtually independent of central government for nearly four decades'; the chiefs 'usually controlled the region ... focused on the city of Ardabil and smaller urban centers' until Reza Khan's army pacified them in winter-spring 1922-23; a Russian force of 5,000 under Gen. Fidarov campaigned against them in 1912. 'none' is kept because Iranica does not describe an acknowledgment of the shah, but 'indirect' is arguable.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Shahsevan' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/shahsevan/)

defacto.controller: Pro-German officers of the Fars Gendarmerie and Democrat Party members (with the Tangestani khans and the German agent Wassmuss as allies)
defacto.note: On 10 Nov 1915 the Gendarmerie seized the government buildings of Shiraz and arrested the British consul (Maj. O'Connor) and the British colony, having 'openly declared with the Germans and revolted against their own Government' (India Office file); Iranica places the expulsion of the British-backed acting governor Habib-Allah Qavam al-Molk in late 1915. His son Ebrahim Khan Qavam al-Molk, with a British-aided tribal army and pro-British gendarmes, took the city back in April 1916 and became acting governor-general. Gendarmes also seized Kerman and Yazd in the same crisis according to Wikipedia, but without dates; not mapped. Added in verification as an omitted rebel-held area of about five months.
sources: India Office Records, File 3516/1914 Pt 18 'German War: Persia; general situation - 1916' and File 334/1916 'Shiraz Prisoners - Major O'Connor', via Qatar Digital Library [search extracts: 10 Nov 1915]
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fars-iv/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qašqāʾi tribal confederacy i' (Qavam al-Molk recaptures Shiraz, Feb-Apr 1916)

defacto.controller: Ismail Agha "Simko" of the Shikak (base at Chehriq castle)
defacto.note: Simko established authority west of Lake Urmia in 1918-19, plundered Urmia in winter 1920, defeated government forces at Tasuj (March 1921) and was joined in summer 1921 by the Mamash, Mangur and Piran. He was defeated by Reza Khan's army in summer 1922 and fled to Iraq; he returned and rebelled again in 1926 and was killed on 30 June 1930 at Ushnu. Persian authority existed only in a few towns.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Simko Shikak revolt (1918-1922)' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Čahrīq' (iranicaonline.org) and 'Khiābāni'/'Great Britain v' extracts on Simko 1920-22 [search extracts]

defacto.controller: Simko and the Shikak
defacto.note: Wikipedia (single source) places Mahabad (Sauj Bulaq) in Simko's hands after the death of Maj. Malakzadeh and about 600 gendarmes in October 1921, with control extending to Sardasht and Baneh by 1922. Treat as low-confidence.

defacto.controller: Local Sistani chiefs (Sarbandi, Kayani maliks; Ali Khan Sarbandi) with Persian and Afghan claims overlapping
defacto.note: Sistan was disputed between Persia and Afghan rulers and run by local chiefs. Ali Khan accepted Persian allegiance in 1857, unpopularly. The Goldsmid arbitration of 1872 awarded Persian (west) Sistan to Persia; Persian governors followed from December 1873.

defacto.note: Iranica: Mir 'Alam Khan drove insurgents out of Sistan and added it to his Qa'enat amirate under Naser al-Din Shah. Sistanis rebelled against the Qa'en chief in Dec 1872 (shut him in Nasirabad); a Persian governor (Samsam al-Mulk, then Mohammad Ja'far Khan, Dec 1873) followed.

defacto.note: British-Indian troops held Sistan to bar German agents from Afghanistan; the Persian governor remained but the force dominated Nasratabad and the border. defacto.note: After the British withdrawal the Alam family governed Sistan and Qa'enat as quasi-hereditary governors: Shawkat al-Molk had full authority in 1921 and resigned in 1924 in favour of two nephews (Iranica). Weakly documented; the 1935 end is a marker only.

defacto.controller: British-officered South Persia Rifles (Sir Percy Sykes) with Indian Army support
defacto.note: Sykes landed at Bandar Abbas in March 1916 to raise the South Persia Rifles (authorised strength 11,000; about 3,300 infantry and 450 cavalry by mid-1917); the force was disbanded in 1921 after the coup. defacto.note: Sykes's column reached Kerman on 12 June 1916 and an SPR brigade was stationed there by December 1916; Persian civil governors remained and the force was disbanded in 1921 after the coup. Same caveat as the Bandar Abbas record (assented under pressure).

defacto.controller: Hereditary governors of Tabas (Mir Hasan Khan 'Vakil-i-Tabas' family; Zangu'i khans; Haji Mohammad Baqer Khan 'Emad al-Molk' under Naser al-Din Shah)
defacto.note: Per the Gazetteer of Persia vol. I (c.1910) the Tabas governorship was hereditary: Nader Shah gave the district to 'Ali Murad Khan of the Zangu'i (Arab, related to the Khozeima amirs of Qa'en) and 'the same family still govern[s] the district'; the older Vakil-i-Tabas family also held it. Haji Mohammad Baqer Khan 'Emad al-Molk' (d. 1894) was succeeded by his eldest son 'Ali Akbar Khan. The khan paid a fixed sum to the shah and was otherwise left to do much as he pleased. The family was still in office around 1910, so the end cannot be earlier; no source for its end was found and 1935 stays a placeholder tied to Pahlavi centralisation.
sources: Gazetteer of Persia vol. I (Government of India, c.1910), via Qatar Digital Library (qdl.qa): Tabas governorship hereditary in the family of Mir Hasan Khan 'Vakil-i-Tabas' [search extract]; also Iranica 'Khorasan xi' extract naming the Zangu'i khans of Tabas

defacto.controller: Anjoman of Tabriz and constitutionalist fighters (Sattar Khan, Baqer Khan)
defacto.note: Tabriz refused Mohammad Ali Shah's coup of 23 June 1908 and withstood a royalist siege for ten months until Russian troops entered on 30 April 1909. The city sought to restore the constitution, not to secede.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Russian occupation of Tabriz' (23 June 1908 rebellion date; cross-check)
Wikipedia, 'Russian occupation of Tabriz' (cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915)

defacto.controller: Imperial Russia (General Snarski's expeditionary force; later Russian garrisons in Tabriz and along the Julfa road)
defacto.note: Russian troops held Tabriz from 30 April 1909; after the Fedayeen attack of 21 Dec 1911 Russia re-entered after shelling on 31 Dec 1911 and executed about 1,200. Russia evacuated on 17 Dec 1914 and the Ottomans (Kurdish irregulars and regulars) held Tabriz 8-31 Jan 1915 (under a month) before Russia returned; last Russians left 28 Feb 1918. Iranian administration continued throughout.
