defacto.controller: Ottoman Empire (IV Corps)
defacto.note: Ottoman forces entered Tabriz on 8 June 1918 (Wikipedia's other date: 18 June) and left after the Armistice of Mudros (30 Oct 1918); exact evacuation date not established.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Persian campaign (World War I)' (cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations)
Wikipedia, 'Russian occupation of Tabriz' (cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915)

defacto.controller: Khans of Tangestan, Dashtestan and Dashti (Zair Khidr, Shaikh Hosein Khan of Chah Kutah) under the governor of Bushehr
defacto.note: Tribal khans of the Bushehr hinterland controlled their districts and acknowledged the Qajars loosely. Baseline characterisation only.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Rais-Ali Delvari' and 'British occupation of Bushehr' (cross-check)
Not independently verified in this research pass; reconstructed from general scholarship

defacto.controller: Tangestani/Dashti tribal forces (Rais Ali Delvari, killed 2 Sept 1915; Shaikh Hosein Khan Chahkutahi; Zair Khidr) with German agent Wassmuss vs. the British and pro-British khans
defacto.note: The tribes attacked the British Residency at Bushehr on 12 July 1915, fought the British after the occupation of Bushehr (8 Aug 1915) and kept the hinterland in revolt, joined by the Qashqai in 1918, until the rising subsided (influenza, British pressure). Some sources say Tangestani resistance lasted to 1921.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Rais-Ali Delvari' and 'British occupation of Bushehr' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fars-iv/)

defacto.controller: Qara'i khans: Eshaq Khan (strangled 8 July 1816) then his son Mohammad Khan (1816-32)
defacto.note: Eshaq Khan Qara'i ruled Torbat-e Heydarieh as a quasi-independent magnate under Fath-Ali Shah (at times effective master of Mohammad-Vali Mirza's Khorasan). Abbas Mirza captured Mohammad Khan by trickery in 1832, ending Qara'i independence; afterwards Qajar-appointed governors ruled.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Esḥāq Khan Qarāʾī' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/eshaq-qarai/) [search extract]
Wikipedia, 'Eshaq Khan Qaraei-Torbati' (cross-check; 8 July 1816 death)
Wikipedia, 'Mohammad Khan Qaraei-Torbati' (cross-check; rule 1816-32, capture 1832)

defacto.controller: Yomut and Goklen (Guklan) tribal leaders
defacto.note: Turkmen of the Gorgan plain raided Khorasan and Astarabad and beat Persian armies (1858 near Qarri-qal'a; 1860 at Merv). Qajar governors of Astarabad held the town and a few forts; the plain itself was outside effective Persian control. Some Goklen paid taxes or migrated under pressure.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Gorgān vii. History from the Safavids to the end of the Pahlavi era' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/gorgan-vii/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Khorasan xi. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/khorasan-xi-history-in-the-qajar-and-pahlavi-periods/)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Guklān' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/guklan/)

defacto.controller: Turkmen tribal chiefs under nominal Persian governors of Astarabad (Persian posts, tax-collection, Russian border pressure)
defacto.note: After the Russian conquest of the Akhal Teke and the Akhal-Khorasan convention (1881) the Yomut/Goklen lost their steppe hinterland and were drawn into limited Persian tax/administrative arrangements. Reza Khan's army moved in and disarmed the Turkmen in 1925; Gonbad-e Qabus became the settlement centre. The 1881 start is a convenience marker.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Gorgān vii. History from the Safavids to the end of the Pahlavi era' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/gorgan-vii/)

defacto.controller: Turkmen People's Councils / Turkmen Cultural and Political Society vs. IRGC
defacto.note: After the Revolution Turkmen councils (shuras) ran local affairs; open clashes in March 1979 ended in a ceasefire on 3 April, with renewed fighting in May and August 1979 and in February 1980; by early 1980 the IRGC had occupied the Turkmen towns. The councils did not secede, and control of towns flipped; included for completeness at low confidence.
sources: Wikipedia, '1979 Turkmen rebellion in Iran' and '1979 Iranian ethnic unrest' (cross-check; no better source found)
Wikipedia, '1979 Iranian ethnic unrest' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Sheikh Ubeydullah of Nehri and his Kurdish tribal host (Ottoman and Iranian Kurds) vs. Qajar forces from Tabriz
defacto.note: Tens of thousands of Kurds crossed into north-west Persia in autumn 1880, took Sauj Bulaq (Mahabad) and Maragheh, failed to take Urmia (its Shia population refused to surrender) and withdrew after about eight weeks. Exact start/end dates not fixed in the sources consulted. Verification: Wikipedia ('Uprising of Sheikh Ubeydullah') says Ubeydullah's son Abdulqadir 'retreated to Mahabad, which they held for a few days' before Qajar forces from Tabriz arrived, and that after about eight weeks the rebels retreated; Urmia held out. Control was transient and set up no administration, so the status is changed from 'none' to 'contested' (low).
sources: Wikipedia, 'Uprising of Sheikh Ubeydullah' (cross-check; ~8 weeks, Mahabad and Maragheh taken, Urmia held out)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, extract on Sheikh Ubeydullah's 1298/1880 invasion of Azarbaijan (iranicaonline.org, 'Kurdish language ii' / 'Safavid dynasty (cont.)' search results)
Wikipedia, 'Uprising of Sheikh Ubeydullah' (cross-check; Mahabad held a few days; withdrawal after eight weeks)

defacto.controller: Imperial Russia (Cossack and line garrisons at Urmia, Khoy and Salmas)
defacto.note: Wikipedia ('Persian campaign (World War I)') says Russia occupied Tabriz in 1909 and Urmia and Khoy in 1910 to secure the road from Julfa to Van; Russian consulates and garrisons controlled the Urmia plain until the Russian withdrawal of Jan-Mar 1918. In Dec 1914 the Russians pulled back to one brigade around Salmas and Urmia and the Ottomans held Urmia from 4 Jan 1915 and briefly Salmas/Dilman; the Russians returned from early Feb 1915 (the Tabriz record treats the same break as under two months). Persian civil administration continued. Added in verification as an omission; start month and extent are approximate (Salmas on the strength of the 1915 fighting at Dilman).
sources: Wikipedia, 'Persian campaign (World War I)' (cross-check; Russian occupation of Urmia and Khoy in 1910; Dec 1914 withdrawal; Jan-Mar 1915)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Russia i. Russo-Iranian Relations up to the Bolshevik Revolution' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/russia-i-relations/) [Russian withdrawal Dec 1917-Mar 1918]

defacto.controller: Assyrian/Armenian forces, Simko's Shikak and local Persian notables after Russia's withdrawal
defacto.note: Russian troops left Azerbaijan between Jan and March 1918. Simko murdered the Assyrian patriarch Mar Shimun on 3 March 1918; Assyrians, Armenians and Kurds fought for the Urmia plain until the Ottomans arrived. Control was fragmented and short-lived.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Russia i. Russo-Iranian Relations up to the Bolshevik Revolution' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/russia-i-relations/)
Wikipedia, 'Simko Shikak revolt (1918-1922)' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Ottoman Empire (IV Corps)
defacto.note: Dilman (Salmas) fell on 18 June and Urmia on 31 July 1918; Ottoman forces left after the Armistice of Mudros (30 Oct 1918).
sources: Wikipedia, 'Persian campaign (World War I)' (cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations)

defacto.controller: United Kingdom (Persia and Iraq Force), later joined by the US Persian Gulf Command (from Dec 1942) in Khuzestan
defacto.note: British forces entered Khuzestan, took Abadan and the Ahvaz oilfields and advanced from Iraq via Kermanshah to Hamadan in Aug-Sept 1941. Iranian administration continued. The Allies withdrew from Tehran on 17 Oct 1941; British (and US) troops left by 2 March 1946 under the Tripartite Treaty.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran' (cross-check)
Wikipedia, 'Iran crisis of 1946' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Soviet Union (44th and 47th Armies)
defacto.note: Soviet troops took Tabriz and Ardabil by 26 Aug 1941. Iranian civil administration continued; the Tripartite Treaty (29 Jan 1942) declared the presence not an occupation and required withdrawal within six months of the end of hostilities (2 March 1946).
sources: Wikipedia, 'Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Azarbaijan v. History from 1941 to 1947' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/azerbaijan-v/)

defacto.controller: Azerbaijan People's Government (Democratic Party of Azerbaijan; Ja'far Pishevari, premier) under Soviet protection
defacto.note: The Democrats took Tabriz around 20-21 Nov 1945 and proclaimed the Autonomous Government of Azerbaijan on 12 Dec 1945 while Soviet troops blocked the Iranian army. Soviet forces left in May 1946; Iranian forces began moving in on 9 Dec 1946 and entered Tabriz on 12-13 Dec 1946, when Pishevari fled to Baku. Dating: Iranica ('Azarbaijan v') says all major routes into the province were seized by the Democrats by 19 Nov 1945, an Iranian column of 1,500 troops was stopped at Qazvin by the Soviets, and Tabriz was 'in the hands of the Democratic Party' by 10 Dec 1945; Wikipedia has 21 Nov. The Soviet-held zone therefore reached the Qazvin line. The Zanjan province units were included by the original researcher; Iranica does not name Zanjan, so their inclusion is unverified (the Iranian advance of Dec 1946 is said to have moved on Zanjan, but no source was found here).
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Azarbaijan v. History from 1941 to 1947' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/azerbaijan-v/)
Wikipedia, 'Iran crisis of 1946' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Soviet Union (based at Mashhad and Bojnurd)
defacto.note: Soviet troops entered Khorasan on 3 Shahrivar 1320 (25 Aug 1941) from Sarakhs, Dargaz and Bajgiran and occupied the north-east, based at Mashhad and Bojnurd; Iranian civil administration continued. CORRECTION: Iranica ('Khorasan xi') says the Soviets stayed 'until the winter of 1943', but the Soviet communique of 25 Feb 1946 announced that evacuation of 'Meshed, Shahrud and Semnan' would begin on 2 March 1946, and on 24-25 March the Soviets (via Kennan, FRUS) said it 'has already been finished' (Mossadegh doubted this on 3-4 March). 'Winter of 1943' is probably a mis-conversion of winter 1324 Sh. (1945-46). The end date is the Soviet claim of completion; the south-east (Birjand, Tabas) was not in the Soviet zone.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Khorasan xi. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/khorasan-xi-history-in-the-qajar-and-pahlavi-periods/)

defacto.controller: Soviet Union
defacto.note: Soviet forces took Gilan (Anzali, Rasht), Mazandaran and Gorgan in August 1941 and reached Qazvin; they entered Tehran on 17 Sept 1941 and withdrew from it by 17 Oct. Iranian civil administration continued. The last Soviet troops left on about 6-9 May 1946. Verification: Semnan province was split into i_wwii_soviet_semnan (evacuated by 24 March 1946); this record now covers Gilan, Mazandaran, Golestan and Qazvin, held to about 6-9 May 1946.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Azarbaijan v. History from 1941 to 1947' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/azerbaijan-v/)
Wikipedia, 'Iran crisis of 1946' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Soviet Union
defacto.note: Soviet forces held Semnan province (Shahrud, Damghan, Semnan) on the Tehran-Mashhad route from the August 1941 invasion; Iranian civil administration continued. Evacuation of Shahrud and Semnan began on 2 March 1946 and was reported finished by 24-25 March (FRUS 1946 VII, doc. 282). Split from the other Soviet-held provinces, which were evacuated until about 6-9 May 1946.
sources: FRUS 1946 vol. VII, doc. 282, Kennan to Secretary of State, 25 Mar 1946 (history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1946v07/d282): Soviet statement that evacuation of Meshed, Shahrud and Semnan, begun 2 Mar 1946, was finished

defacto.controller: Babis led by Mulla Mohammad-'Ali Hojjat al-Eslam Zanjani (about 2,000 fighters and their families) vs. the governor and the shah's army
defacto.note: The Zanjan 'upheaval' began on 13 May 1850; from about 19 May the town was divided in two, with the Babis holding their fortified quarters against the governor and then against the army that gathered from June (Aziz Khan Mokri, commander-in-chief, arrived on 25 Aug). Hojjat died on 29 Dec and the last Babi positions fell in a general assault about 2 Jan 1851. Added in verification as an omitted eight-month armed enclave; coded contested because the town was split rather than ceded to a separate government. The Babi stand at Shaykh Tabarsi (Mazandaran, late 1848-May 1849) and the Neyriz rising (1850) were also armed enclaves but were not mapped (single fort / weeks).
sources: 'The Babi Uprising in Zanjan: Causes and Issues', Iranian Studies (cambridge.org/core/journals/iranian-studies/article/babi-uprising-in-zanjan-causes-and-issues/D3DA0EDE843431436706E292F3B62AD9) [search extract]

events.summary: Under a Persian firman of 1793 (lease of 1794) the Sultan of Muscat administered Bandar Abbas, the coast from Minab to Khamir and the islands of Qeshm and Hormuz for 75 years. The arrangement was contested in 1804-10 by Mulla Hosein of Qeshm and the Qawasim and was restricted to 20 years from 1855.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti' (cross-check)

events.title: Qajars retake Mashhad from Nader Mirza Afshar
events.summary: After failed attempts in 1799 and 1801 and a personal campaign in 1802, Fath-Ali Shah's forces under Mohammad-Vali Mirza entered Mashhad in early 1803. Nader Mirza was taken to Tehran and executed; Khorasan came under Qajar control, though local khans kept wide autonomy.

events.summary: Fath-Ali Shah's forces defeated Firuz al-Din Mirza (battle of Shahdih, 1807); tribute exacted and Persian suzerainty (claimed since c.1801) reasserted, repeated 1814.

events.title: Treaty of Gulistan
events.summary: Signed 12 Oct OS (24 Oct NS; Iranica: 29 Shawwal 1228) at Gulistan; ratified at Tbilisi Sept 1814. Persia recognised Russian sovereignty over Georgia (with Shuragel), Daghestan, Karabakh, Ganja, Shaki, Shirvan, Derbent, Quba, Baku and Talysh (frontier left to commissioners), and Russian-held lands generally. Gokcha/Sevan and Erivan stayed Persian; the vague frontier fuelled the 1826 war.

events.summary: Abbas Mirza crossed at Gurbulak (16 Sept 1821), stormed Bayezid in Nov 1821 and beat the Ottomans at Toprakkale (May 1822); Mohammad Ali Mirza took Shahrizor and Sulaymaniyah and besieged Baghdad until he died of cholera on 22 Nov 1822.

events.title: Russia occupies north shore of Lake Gokcha
events.summary: Yermolov seized the northern bank of Lake Gokcha (Sevan) in early 1825, claiming Gulistan allowed it; Iran protested and the occupation became the main grievance behind the 1826 war. The Russian war manifesto conceded Persia's right to the district.

events.title: Russo-Persian war reopens; Persian counter-offensive
events.summary: Abbas Mirza's army crossed the Aras in July 1826 (Russia took Bash-Aparan on 8 July; Persia took Pambak/Shuragel late July). Local uprisings in Talysh, Shirvan, Ganja and elsewhere helped Persia retake most Gulistan-ceded lands in summer 1826. Because Tehran had renounced these lands in 1813, they are mapped as 'iranian_held', not as restored claims, although the war's aim was to reverse Gulistan.

events.summary: After six days' fighting from 25 July 1826 OS the Russian garrison abandoned Lankaran (31 July OS = 12 Aug NS); Iranian forces also took Salyan. Russia retook the Talysh coast later in 1826 (exact date unverified; Wikipedia's Lankaran article claims Persian retention until 1828).

events.summary: Mishchenko defeated Mostafa Khan and Persian regulars; Shirvan, which had gone over to Mostafa Khan about 4 Aug, returned to Russia.
